stem:
In an investigation, the volume of oxygen that combined with haemoglobin at different partial pressures of oxygen was determined. The results are shown in Fig. 5.1.

{{figure:figure_5_1.webp}}

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem:
The partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli is $13.3\text{kPa}$. At this partial pressure of oxygen the **total volume of oxygen** that is carried by $100\text{cm}^3$ blood is $19.78\text{cm}^3$ at pH 7.4 and $37^\circ\text{C}$.

The volume of oxygen that combines with haemoglobin at $13.3\text{kPa}$ is $19.48\text{cm}^3$ $100\text{cm}^{-3}$ blood.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of oxygen that is combined with haemoglobin in $100\text{cm}^3$ blood.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Suggest how the oxygen that is **not** combined with haemoglobin is transported in the blood.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text: Explain why a long-term smoker would have a lower volume of oxygen combined with haemoglobin in the alveoli at $13.3\text{kPa}$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Describe the role of carbonic anhydrase in the transport of carbon dioxide.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The investigation was repeated in the presence of carbon dioxide. The volumes of oxygen combined with haemoglobin at partial pressures of oxygen below $8.0\text{kPa}$ were less than shown in Fig. 5.1.

Name this effect **and** explain the advantage of this decrease at partial pressures of oxygen below $8.0\text{kPa}$.
